title: Getting Started
intro: The machine-learning ground you need for quantum reservoir computing, taught from zero, ending with a complete quantum reservoir worked by hand. Six pages: what reservoir computing is, time series and prediction, neural networks, linear regression and the ridge readout, training and testing, and a two-qubit reservoir computed with numbers.

blocks.text: Quantum reservoir computing sits where two fields meet: machine learning, which supplies the task and the readout, and quantum mechanics, which supplies the reservoir. The chapters that follow this one, on foundations, open systems, models, hardware and theory, move quickly between the two. They assume you know what a time series is, what a recurrent network does, what it means to fit a readout by regression, how a result is scored on data it has not seen, and what a small quantum reservoir looks like when you work it out. This chapter teaches those five things from nothing, then puts them together in one complete example.

You need no machine learning. You do not need the Quantum Mechanics shelf for the first five pages; the sixth uses qubits, density matrices and measurement, and says which pages of that shelf it relies on at each step. Algebra at school level is enough throughout, and where a little calculus is used (a derivative as a rate of change) it is explained on the spot. Every page does its arithmetic with real numbers, in the order a person would do it with pencil and calculator, and gives a code sample that reproduces them.

Read the six pages in order. Each one assumes the ones before it, and the last one ties them together. Each page opens with what you need first and what you will be able to do, ends each main section with a 'Check yourself' question, and finishes with problems that have full solutions. The check questions are short; do them before reading on. Plan on one to two hours per page, six to ten hours for the chapter, more if you work every problem and run every code sample. If you already know machine learning, read the first page for the picture and the last for the quantum model, and skim the middle four for the notation and the tasks.

items: What Is Reservoir Computing? (#/qrc/start/what-is-reservoir-computing): the problem of signals that unfold in time, the water-ripple picture and where it breaks, the three parts (input, fixed reservoir, trained readout), why training only the readout is cheap, and one paragraph each on physical and quantum reservoirs. No mathematics, but a buckets-with-holes reservoir you can follow by hand and a map of the whole library.

Time Series and Prediction (#/qrc/start/time-series-and-prediction): sequences, sampling, lags and windows, one-step-ahead prediction, baselines and error measures computed by hand, and the three tasks (delay recall, a product of past inputs, NARMA2 worked term by term) that separate memory from nonlinearity.

Neural Networks from Scratch (#/qrc/start/neural-networks-primer): a neuron computed by hand, layers and a forward pass, training by gradient descent with a worked step, recurrent networks unrolled for three steps, why gradients through time vanish or explode, and how reservoir computing sidesteps the problem.

Linear Regression and the Ridge Readout (#/qrc/start/linear-regression-and-ridge): fitting a line by least squares, the normal equations derived step by step, many features as a matrix, overfitting with numbers, the ridge penalty and how to choose it. This is exactly the readout of a reservoir.

Training, Testing and Measuring Error (#/qrc/start/training-and-testing): training, validation and test data, why the start of a run (the washout) is discarded, NMSE by hand, memory capacity as a score, how to spot overfitting, and a complete small echo state experiment in numpy.

A Quantum Reservoir Worked by Hand (#/qrc/start/quantum-reservoir-by-hand): two qubits, a fixed Hamiltonian, an input written into the first qubit, evolution, readout of the average $z$ spin of each qubit; three time steps with numbers, then a few hundred steps in numpy with a ridge readout on a delay task.

blocks.text: These are the equations the chapter builds up to. Each says what it means in one line; the pages say where it comes from.

blocks.tex: z = w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + \dots + b, \qquad a = f(z)
blocks.caption: A neuron: a weighted sum plus a bias, bent by an activation function f such as tanh.
A recurrent network: the new state mixes the old state and the new input. In a reservoir W, v and b are random and never trained.
NARMA2, the benchmark that needs memory (feedback terms) and nonlinearity (the product and the cube).
The readout: a weighted sum of the reservoir state numbers. Only the weights w are learned.
The ridge solution: the weights that best fit the targets y from the table X of states, with a penalty lambda that keeps them small. The normal equations are the case lambda = 0.
The error score: squared error divided by the variance of the target; 1 means no better than the average, 0 means perfect.
A quantum reservoir state: the average z spin of qubit i in the density matrix rho(k). These numbers are the features the readout weighs.

blocks.text: After this chapter the library goes deeper into one topic at a time. Reservoir Computing Foundations (#/qrc/foundations) develops the classical theory: echo state networks, the echo state property, memory capacity, physical reservoirs and benchmarks. Open Quantum Systems Toolkit (#/qrc/open-systems) gives the language for quantum systems that lose information to their surroundings. Quantum Reservoir Models (#/qrc/models) covers the spin-network reservoir, input encoding and readout. Measurement and Hardware (#/qrc/hardware) and Theory, Limits and Practice (#/qrc/theory) cover what real devices can do, what is provable, and an open list of problems.

If you are short of time and know some machine learning, read Training, Testing and Measuring Error (#/qrc/start/training-and-testing) for the washout and scoring conventions this library uses everywhere, and A Quantum Reservoir Worked by Hand (#/qrc/start/quantum-reservoir-by-hand) for the model that the rest of the quantum chapters elaborate.
